explanations.explanation: Jeremiah's message says "whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans will live" (Jer 38:2). It even adds that he will keep his life "like a spoil of war." So the one who gives up is the one who comes out with something. That sounds backwards, friend, but it's what the LORD's word says.

That's a brave instinct, but this message doesn't offer it. In Jeremiah 38:2 the ones who stay in the city die by sword and famine and plague, and the ones who surrender live. Fighting isn't named as a way to live. I know surrendering sounds like the opposite of winning, friend, but that's the word Jeremiah gives.

Egypt never comes up in this message. The LORD's word in Jeremiah 38:2 gives two paths: stay in the city and die by sword and famine and plague, or surrender to the Chaldeans and live. Running off somewhere else just isn't on the list.

Jeremiah says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, "This city will surely be delivered into the hands of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it" (Jer 38:3). The word "never" isn't anywhere in that sentence. It's a hard message, and the text says it plainly.

The message goes the other way. The LORD says, "This city will surely be delivered into the hands of the army of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it" (Jer 38:3). So "never" is the sneaky word on this card. When a card hands you "never" or "always," check the verse twice, like checking the oven before you pull the tray.

The officials say it right to the king: "This man ought to die" (Jer 38:4). Their reason is that Jeremiah is discouraging the warriors who remain in the city and all the people with his words. They also say he isn't seeking the people's well-being but their ruin. This part is heavy, so I'll say it plainly and let it sit.

Exile isn't what they ask for. They tell the king, "This man ought to die" (Jer 38:4). That's a heavy line, and I won't joke over it. Their reason is that Jeremiah is discouraging the warriors who remain and all the people.

Nobody mentions a whipping. What the officials tell the king is "This man ought to die" (Jer 38:4). It's a heavy thing to say about anyone, so I'll leave it plain. They point to his words discouraging the warriors and the people as their reason.

Zedekiah answers, "He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you" (Jer 38:5). He hands Jeremiah over in his own words. I think that sounds like a boss pointing at someone else's desk, though the text doesn't say what he felt. A king saying he can do nothing is a lot to hear, friend.
Zedekiah doesn't say that. He says, "He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you" (Jer 38:5). He doesn't take Jeremiah on himself. He gives the officials the say.

No release comes from the king here. Zedekiah says, "He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you" (Jer 38:5). Those words are about as far from "let him go" as you can get, friend. The officials hear a king who says he can't stop them.

Mud. The cistern had "no water but only mud," and Jeremiah sank down into it (Jer 38:6). I spent years stuck in the back of a junk drawer with paper and dust, and I'd still pick that over this. Friend, being stuck is one thing, but sinking is another.
Sand isn't in the verse. The cistern had "no water but only mud" (Jer 38:6). Sand you can at least shake out of your shoes, friend. Mud holds on, and Jeremiah sank down into it.

No ash down there. The verse says the cistern had "no water but only mud" (Jer 38:6). I've scraped enough burnt cookie bottoms to know ash when I see it, and this was a different mess. Jeremiah sank down into the mud.

Ebed-melech says, "My lord the king, these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet" (Jer 38:9). He says it plainly to the king himself. No sprinkles on it, no frosting, just the plain word. I think that took nerve.

It's right there in the text. Ebed-melech tells the king, "these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet" (Jer 38:9). He says it to the king at the Gate of Benjamin (Jer 38:7-8). I think it took some nerve to say that out loud, friend.

explanations.answer: There is no more bread in the city
explanations.explanation: Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve "for there is no more bread in the city" (Jer 38:9). That fits the famine named in Jeremiah 38:2. Plain reason, plainly said, and it's the only one he gives.

explanations.answer: The officials took away his food
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve "for there is no more bread in the city" (Jer 38:9). He doesn't say anyone took food from Jeremiah. I'd call that a whole-city problem, not a Jeremiah-only problem.

explanations.answer: The guards are not allowed to feed him
explanations.explanation: No rule about guards is mentioned. Ebed-melech says the reason is "there is no more bread in the city" (Jer 38:9). Nobody in the passage is said to be forbidden from feeding him. It's about the city running out, which fits the famine in Jeremiah 38:2.

Zedekiah does the opposite of turning him down. He answers, "Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies" (Jer 38:10). Earlier the king said he could do nothing, and now he gives an order. That's a yes, and a big one.

Zedekiah says yes and gives an order: "Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies" (Jer 38:10). This is the same king who said earlier he could do nothing to stop the officials (Jer 38:5). Ebed-melech spoke up, and the king gave the command, friend.

Ebed-melech calls down, "Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes" (Jer 38:12). So it's rags between Jeremiah's arms and the rope while they pull him up out of the mud. Jeremiah does so, and then they lift him out (Jer 38:12-13). I think that's a thoughtful touch, friend.

explanations.answer: To keep warm in the mud
explanations.explanation: Warmth isn't what the text says. The rags were "to pad the ropes" (Jer 38:12). They went under Jeremiah's arms, between him and the ropes. A blanket might have been nice, but the verse says what the rags were for.

Wiping isn't the job. Ebed-melech says the rags are "to pad the ropes" (Jer 38:12). Jeremiah puts them under his arms, and then the men pull him up. A whole stack of rags wouldn't wipe up that much mud anyway, friend.

Out of the cistern isn't the same as set free. The text says, "And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard" (Jer 38:13). That's the same courtyard where the cistern was (Jer 38:6). He's out of the mud, but he's still in the guard's courtyard.

Jeremiah 38:13 says, "And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard." The cistern was in that courtyard to begin with (Jer 38:6). So he goes from the mud to the courtyard, which is a big step up but not freedom. Dry ground is still a win, friend.

explanations.answer: The king will surely put him to death
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah says, "If I tell you, you will surely put me to death" (Jer 38:15). That's a heavy thing to say to a king's face. I think a man who just came out of a cistern has reason to be careful with his words.

explanations.answer: The king will throw him back in the cistern
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess after the cistern, but Jeremiah says something else. His words are, "you will surely put me to death" (Jer 38:15). The cistern isn't in his answer. He names death.

explanations.answer: The king will send him off to Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon doesn't come up in his answer. His worry is "you will surely put me to death" (Jer 38:15). That's a heavy thing to say to a king, so I'll leave it at that.

explanations.answer: He will not kill him or hand him over
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah swears, "As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life" (Jer 38:16). He swears it secretly, and he swears by the LORD. That's two promises in one breath: no killing and no handing over. It answers the fear Jeremiah just named in the verse before.

explanations.answer: He will send him away from the city
explanations.explanation: Sending Jeremiah away isn't part of the oath. Zedekiah swears, "I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life" (Jer 38:16). It's all about keeping him alive and out of those men's hands. He swears it secretly, by the LORD.

explanations.answer: He will do whatever the LORD says
explanations.explanation: His oath is about Jeremiah's life, not about what he'll do with the LORD's word. Zedekiah says, "I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life" (Jer 38:16). Nothing in it promises to follow what the LORD says. In verse 19 he comes back with a fear.

The LORD says that if Zedekiah surrenders to the officers of Babylon's king, "you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive" (Jer 38:17). Notice the promise goes beyond the king, because his household survives too. The city stays standing. That's a lot of good riding on one choice, friend.

The word is "burned down," not abandoned (Jer 38:17). The LORD says if Zedekiah surrenders, "this city will not be burned down." So the city is still standing, and the king and his household survive. Abandoned is a fine word, just not the one in the verse.

Emptied doesn't match. The LORD says "this city will not be burned down" (Jer 38:17). Fire is the word in the verse, and it comes up again in verse 18. If he surrenders, the king and his household survive too.

If Zedekiah refuses, the LORD says the opposite: "you yourself will not escape their grasp" (Jer 38:18). The city will be delivered into the hands of the Chaldeans, and they will burn it down. So there's no escape for him on that road. It's the other half of the choice, and it's the heavy half.

Right, he won't escape. The LORD says, "you yourself will not escape their grasp" (Jer 38:18). The city goes into the hands of the Chaldeans, and they burn it down. That's the "if you don't" side of the choice, laid out plain.

explanations.answer: The Jews who deserted to the Chaldeans
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah says he's afraid of "the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans," because the Chaldeans may deliver him into their hands to abuse him (Jer 38:19). That's the fear he names, in his own words. I think fear can talk louder than a promise, though the text doesn't say what else he felt. It's a very human spot to be in, friend.

explanations.answer: The prophets who spoke against Jeremiah
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah doesn't name any prophets. He says he is afraid of "the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans" (Jer 38:19). His worry is that the Chaldeans may hand him over to them. Different group, friend.

Pharaoh's army doesn't show up in his answer. The fear he names is "the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans" (Jer 38:19). He says the Chaldeans may deliver him into their hands to abuse him. Keep your eye on the verse, baker.

Jeremiah says it flat: "They will not hand you over" (Jer 38:20). Then he adds, "Obey the voice of the LORD in what I am telling you, that it may go well with you and you may live." He answers the king's fear with the LORD's word and an appeal to obey. Short answer, big weight.

It's in the text. Jeremiah answers the king's fear straight: "They will not hand you over" (Jer 38:20). Then he tells Zedekiah to obey the voice of the LORD so that it may go well with him and he may live. So Jeremiah isn't leaving the king's fear hanging, friend.

The women will say, "Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you" (Jer 38:22). Mud again, friend, but this time it's the king's feet. In that picture, his trusted friends are the ones who leave. Jeremiah says this is what the LORD has shown him (Jer 38:21).

Rescued isn't in the line. The women say "they deserted you" (Jer 38:22). Those trusted friends leave instead of helping. Rescue would have been a nicer ending for the king, but that's not the picture here.
Warned isn't the word. The women say "they deserted you" (Jer 38:22). It's about trusted friends who left when his feet sank into the mire. Walking away isn't a warning, friend.

Jeremiah says, "All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans" (Jer 38:23). He also says Zedekiah himself will not escape and the city will be burned down. This is one of the heaviest lines in the passage, so I'll say it simply and leave it. It's what comes if he refuses to surrender (Jer 38:21).

That line is in the text, and it's heavy. Jeremiah says, "All your wives and children will be brought out to the Chaldeans" (Jer 38:23). It's said about what happens if Zedekiah refuses to surrender (Jer 38:21). I'll leave it plain.

explanations.answer: He asked not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die
explanations.explanation: Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to say, "I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there" (Jer 38:26). Those are the words the king gave him for the officials. When the officials come, Jeremiah relays "the exact words the king had commanded him to say" (Jer 38:27). Short, clear, and nothing extra added.

explanations.answer: He came to report to the king on the officials' plans
explanations.explanation: The king doesn't give him those words. What he tells Jeremiah to say is, "I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there" (Jer 38:26). That's about Jeremiah's own petition to the king. The officials' plans don't come into it.

explanations.answer: He came to pray for the king and the people of the city
explanations.explanation: Praying isn't in the words the king gives. Zedekiah tells him to say, "I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there" (Jer 38:26). It's a petition about Jeremiah's own life. Jeremiah then gives the officials exactly what the king commanded (Jer 38:27).

explanations.answer: No one had overheard the conversation
explanations.explanation: The officials "said no more to him, for no one had overheard the conversation" (Jer 38:27). Jeremiah gave them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. With no one having heard it, they stop there. A secret works best when nobody's listening at the door, friend.

explanations.answer: The king ordered them to leave him alone
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse has the king ordering the officials. The text gives its own reason: "no one had overheard the conversation" (Jer 38:27). The king did tell Jeremiah what to say (Jer 38:26). That's different from commanding the officials.

explanations.answer: They feared what the people might do
explanations.explanation: The people aren't mentioned in this part. The reason is "no one had overheard the conversation" (Jer 38:27). Jeremiah gave them the exact words the king had commanded him to say, and then they said no more to him. Stick to the verse, friend.

Jeremiah stays in the courtyard of the guard "until the day Jerusalem was captured" (Jer 38:28). That's the same word as the LORD's message earlier, that the king of Babylon "will capture it" (Jer 38:3). So this passage ends right at the day the city is captured.

Rebuilt isn't the word. Verse 28 says Jeremiah remained in the courtyard "until the day Jerusalem was captured." That word comes from the LORD's message earlier: "he will capture it" (Jer 38:3). Nobody is building anything in this verse.

Spared goes the other way. The LORD says the king of Babylon "will capture it" (Jer 38:3), and verse 28 reaches "the day Jerusalem was captured." So the city isn't spared in this text. Not the news anybody wanted, friend, but it's what's written.
